name: Teething in babies: signs and what helps
summary: The NHS lists sore red gums, a flushed cheek and extra dribbling as signs of teething, and suggests gum massage or a cool teething ring.
keyPoints: The NHS says teething can cause few or no symptoms, and lists a sore red gum, one flushed cheek, ear-rubbing, dribbling and fretfulness as possible signs.
NHS sources say teething does not usually cause diarrhoea or a high temperature, so those signs may have another cause such as an infection.
A worried parent can contact a GP or call NHS 111, and an emergency such as a fit needs 999.
Suggested comfort measures include gum massage, a cooled teething ring and chilled fruit or vegetables for older babies, with supervision.
Teething gels have little evidence behind them, a pharmacist can advise, and amber necklaces are not recommended.
Tooth cleaning with fluoride toothpaste starts when the first tooth comes through, and the NHS advises registering the baby with a dentist.

body.heading: What are the usual signs of teething?
body.body: Teething is the time when a baby's first teeth, called milk teeth, push through the gums. The NHS says most babies get their first tooth some time in their first year, but the timing varies a lot. Some babies seem to have no discomfort at all, and some teeth come through without any trouble. When there are signs, the NHS lists a sore, red gum where the tooth is coming through and one flushed cheek. Other signs it lists include rubbing an ear, dribbling more than usual, chewing on things and being fretful. One NHS service says most babies start teething at around 6 months, though some start earlier and others later. A baby may also sleep badly, and the NHS mentions a mildly raised temperature of less than 38C.

body.heading: Which symptoms are not caused by teething?
body.body: The NHS and other NHS services say teething does not usually make a baby ill. The NHS 111 Wales page says it does not usually cause diarrhoea or a high temperature. Those signs may have another cause, such as an infection. The NHS also says there is no evidence that teething causes diarrhoea. The NHS 111 Wales page also covers a baby who seems unwell or in distress, or whose condition is getting worse.

body.heading: When should a parent get medical help?
body.body: The NHS says a GP can be contacted, or NHS 111 called, if a symptom is worrying. A local NHS page lists a high temperature in a very young baby, a fit, going blue or blotchy, being very pale and a spotty purple-red rash as red flags. A baby with a fit needs emergency help, which means calling 999. A baby who seems unusually listless and unhappy may have something other than teething, and a high fever should be checked by a GP. Sources say a high temperature in a baby is a reason to contact a GP or NHS 111 rather than assume teething.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest to ease teething?
body.body: The NHS suggests gently rubbing the baby's gum with a clean finger. A teething ring can help, and it can be cooled in the fridge. The NHS says a ring should not be put in the freezer, and should never be tied around a baby's neck. A clean, cold, wet flannel is another idea. For babies of 6 months or older, the NHS mentions chilled pieces of fruit or vegetables such as banana, cucumber or melon. These should be given with supervision, because a baby could choke. Rusks are best avoided, as nearly all brands contain some sugar.

body.heading: What about teething gels and medicines?
body.body: The NHS says there is little evidence that teething gels work, so the comfort measures above come first. If a gel is used, it should be one made for young children. Homeopathic teething gels have no evidence of working, and any used should be licensed in the UK. GOV.UK reports that teething gels containing a local anaesthetic are sold from pharmacies only, with the MHRA advising use after advice from a pharmacist or other health professional. The MHRA also says gels with salicylate are no longer suitable for children under 16 for teething pain. NHS pages also mention paracetamol or ibuprofen for babies who are old enough and still in pain. A pharmacist can advise on which choice suits a baby and the right product for their age.

body.heading: Are amber teething necklaces recommended?
body.body: One NHS page says there is no proof that amber jewellery eases teething pain. Such items are described as a choking and strangulation risk, and the page says they should not be used. This fits the NHS advice that nothing, including a teething ring, should be put around a baby's neck.

body.heading: When should tooth cleaning start, and when is the dentist involved?
body.body: The NHS says brushing starts as soon as the first milk tooth breaks through. It describes a baby toothbrush with a tiny smear of fluoride toothpaste, and brushing twice a day, including last thing at night. For children under 3 the NHS describes a smear of toothpaste, and from age 3 to 6 an amount about the size of a pea. The NHS says a parent or carer should do the brushing and should not rinse the mouth afterwards, so that the fluoride stays on the teeth. The NHS says a baby should be registered with a dentist when the teeth start coming through. NHS dental care for children is free, though not every dentist takes on new NHS patients, and nhs.uk has a search for NHS dentists. Local services differ on the timing of the first dental visit, so a health visitor or dentist can say what applies locally.
